/*
# SimpleLayout — stack children along an axis

The stacking idiom: siblings placed one after another along
`axis`, in child order, `spacing` apart (negative overlaps). The cross axis
and all sizes stay the children's own — a child centers itself across a row
with the ordinary `y = center`. Invisible children are skipped and their
space reclaimed; a skipped child still gets the slot it would occupy, so
re-showing it needs no special case. A `Spacer` child flexes to absorb the
run's slack along the axis (between two groups it pushes them apart; one on
each side centers the run).

Written in Declare over the Layout kernel: the whole strategy is this one
pure place() — one box per laid child, aligned by index.

**Padding is the view's** (`View.padding`), and this stack obeys it without
knowing it exists: it arranges inside the room the view gives it, so a run
placed at `0` starts at the content origin, the cross-axis band `align` works
in is the room *between* the insets, and a view that sizes itself from the
stack grows by both. The inset reaches **every** child, on both axes,
`align = none` included — a child placing its own `x = 0` sits on the content
edge, not the view's, because the content box is the parent's and not this
arrangement's.

```declare
col: View [ x = 20, y = 20,
    layout: SimpleLayout [ axis = y, spacing = 8 ],
    View [ width = 160, height = 24, cornerRadius = 6, fill = steelblue ],
    View [ width = 120, height = 24, cornerRadius = 6, fill = cadetblue ],
    View [ width = 190, height = 24, cornerRadius = 6, fill = slategray ]
    ]
```

## axis
Which way children stack: `y` (the default) or `x`. **A bare literal, not a string** —
`axis = x`, and note that `x` here is the axis token, not the position attribute.

## spacing
The gap between adjacent children. **Negative overlaps them**, which is how a stack of
cards or avatars is built.

## align
The **cross axis** — `y` on a row, `x` on a stack. `none` (the default) leaves it to the
children, who place themselves with the ordinary `y = center`. `start | center | end`
aligns every child within the **band**: the view's own cross **content** extent — so a
column `width = 260` centres a `width = { parent.width - 32 }` child at 16, with the slack
split evenly — falling back to the **line**, the tallest (widest) laid child's extent, on a view
that derives its own cross size from these very children (reading an extent this
arrangement feeds would be a cycle, and on such a view the line *is* that extent). A
child wider than the band keeps the line, so it never hangs out both sides.
`baseline` — a row only — sits every child on one
baseline: a `Text` reports its own, and a composite **declares** which part carries it
(`baseline: number = { cap.y + cap.baseline }`); a laid child that declares none is
refused by name, at the child, and the checker says so before anything runs. A bare
literal.

## place()
The whole strategy: one box per laid child, positioned along the axis in child order.
**Every size stays the children's own, and so does the cross axis unless `align` says
otherwise** — then the boxes carry that slot too, and own it. Override it in a subclass
for custom geometry; a `Layout`'s `place()` **may** aggregate over children, which is the
one place that is allowed.
*/

class SimpleLayout extends Layout [
    axis: Axis = y,
    spacing: number = 0,
    align: CrossAlign = none,

    place() {
        const axis = this.axis
        const size = axis == "x" ? "width" : "height"
        const kids = this.laid()
        const flexing = (c) => (c).flexes === true

        // slack, only when someone flexes: the view's extent along the axis
        // minus the rigid content and the gaps between visible children.
        // A child's slot is its footprint (the scale/rotation-composed box),
        // so a scale = 0.5 child occupies half the run and a rotated card
        // reserves what it visibly covers; the box's lead compensates the
        // transform's own offset so the visible edge lands on the slot
        let each = 0
        let flexN = 0
        for (const c of kids) if (c.visible && flexing(c)) flexN = flexN + 1
        if (flexN > 0) {
            let content = 0
            let visN = 0
            for (const c of kids) {
                if (!c.visible) continue
                visN = visN + 1
                if (!flexing(c)) content = content + (c).footprint()[size]
            }
            const extent = this.contentExtent(size)
            each = Math.max(0, (extent - content - this.spacing * Math.max(0, visN - 1)) / flexN)
        }

        // the cross axis, when `align` claims it: children align within the
        // BAND — the view's own cross extent, or the largest laid cross extent
        // when the view measures these very children (viewExtent answers 0 on
        // that view: reading an extent this pass feeds is the cycle the
        // one-pass discipline forbids, and there the two agree anyway).
        // Math.max keeps an over-wide child from hanging out both sides.
        // A baseline line is the deepest declared one.
        const al = this.align
        const cross = axis == "x" ? "y" : "x"
        const crossSize = axis == "x" ? "height" : "width"
        let line = 0
        let lineBase = 0
        if (al != "none") {
            if (al == "baseline" && axis != "x") this.refuseStackBaseline()
            for (const c of kids) {
                if (!c.visible) continue
                line = Math.max(line, (c).footprint()[crossSize])
                const b = (c).baseline
                if (al == "baseline" && typeof b == "number") lineBase = Math.max(lineBase, b)
            }
            // `start` places at the band's origin and `baseline` on the shared
            // line — neither reads the band, so only center/end ask for it
            if (al == "center" || al == "end") line = Math.max(line, this.viewExtent(crossSize))
        }

        let pos = 0
        return kids.map((c) => {
            const flex = c.visible && flexing(c)
            // footprint, never bounds: the strategy must not read the slot it
            // writes (one-pass discipline). A flexing child's size is allocated
            // (box.w/h), so its footprint is never consulted — lead 0, raw slot.
            const f = flex ? null : (c).footprint()
            const lead = f == null ? 0 : (axis == "x" ? f.x : f.y)
            const box = (axis == "x" ? ({ x: pos - lead }) : ({ y: pos - lead }))
            if (flex) box[axis == "x" ? "w" : "h"] = each
            if (al != "none") {
                // start = the line's origin; center/end offset the child's
                // footprint within the line; baseline sits the child's declared
                // baseline on the line's — a child with none is refused, once,
                // and placed at start (the arrangement never breaks)
                const fc = f == null ? (c).footprint() : f
                const leadC = axis == "x" ? fc.y : fc.x
                let off = 0
                if (al == "center") off = (line - fc[crossSize]) / 2
                else if (al == "end") off = line - fc[crossSize]
                else if (al == "baseline" && axis == "x") {
                    const b = (c).baseline
                    if (typeof b == "number") off = lineBase - b
                    else if (c.visible) this.refuseBaseline(c)
                }
                box[cross] = off - (al == "baseline" ? 0 : leadC)
            }
            if (c.visible) pos = pos + (flex ? each : (f)[size]) + this.spacing
            return box
            })
        }
    ]

/*
# Icon — the drawn mark

A small monochrome mark, **drawn** rather than typed. A font's glyphs are not
marks: they are not guaranteed to be present, they rasterize differently on
every platform, and the ones that exist are the wrong shapes — a `✓` sits on the
text baseline and reads like a square-root sign, not like a checkmark. The
library's own marks — `Checkbox.mark`, `Menu.check`, the `Combobox` disclosure —
are all `Icon`s.

### Writing one

Subclass and override `draw`. Author the shape in a **16×16 box** — `unit`
converts it to whatever size the host asked for:

```declare-fragment
class SparkIcon extends Icon [
    draw(d: Draw) {
        d.scale(unit, unit)
        d.strokeStyle = ink; d.lineWidth = weight / unit
        d.beginPath(); d.moveTo(8, 1); d.lineTo(8, 15); d.stroke()
        }
    ]
```

Overriding a **method** is the refinement path that works — re-opening an
inherited child is not (`cap:` on a `Button` subclass fails at instantiate), so
the shape lives in `draw` and everything adjustable is a slot.

### Size changes the drawing, not the shape

Every icon is **one path**. There are no per-size variants, no thresholds, nothing
redrawn at a breakpoint: `unit` scales the 16-box to whatever the host asked for,
so a 64px icon is the 16px icon at 4×, exactly.

The **stroke** is the deliberate exception. `d.lineWidth = weight / unit` sits
*inside* `d.scale(unit, unit)`, so the two cancel and the line lands at a constant
`weight` in **device pixels at every size**. An icon's line therefore matches the
1px rules and text weights it sits among, instead of fattening as it grows.

The cost is that the stroke-to-size ratio falls: 1.6px is 10% of a 16px icon, 5%
at 32, 2.5% at 64. Across 14–18px — chrome sizes — that is invisible. Past ~32
an icon starts reading as a fine-line drawing rather than a mark — so **this set
is built for chrome sizes**, and a large display icon (an empty-state mark, an
about-box graphic) would want the opposite: `d.lineWidth = weight` *outside* the
scale, so the line grows with the drawing. Real icon systems take a third road
and redraw per optical size range; that is a bigger undertaking than this set
needs.

### What is not an Icon

Application art. The desktop's dock icons are the case to look at before
reaching for this class: they rest at 56px and grow under the magnification
swell, they are polychrome (`gradient(hue1, hue2)` behind a hue-parameterised
drawing), and their **width animates every frame**. Each of those alone rules
them out — the constant stroke that suits a 16px mark is 2.9% of a 56px one and
reads spindly; `ink` is a single colour; and an animated width is the one thing
this set forbids.

The line is not "drawn versus not drawn" — dock art is drawn too. It is
**chrome vocabulary versus identity**. A mark that says *close*, *expand*,
*checked*, *this is the dark theme* belongs here, at a size the host states.
A mark that says *this is Calendar* does not, and belongs to the app that owns
the identity.

Desktop has both, which is what makes it the clarifying example: its menu rows
take `WindowIcon` and `CodeIcon` from this set, while its dock keeps `DockIcon`.

### Two rules

**Scale inside the body, never with the View's `scale`.** A recording rasterizes
into a canvas sized to its own ink bounds at device resolution, while `scale` is
a transform applied *after* — so `scale = { width / 16 }` would rasterize 16
pixels and stretch them. Crisp at exactly 16, soft at every other size, which is
most of them. Scaling inside the recording allocates the raster at true size
instead.

**Never animate an icon's `width`.** Reading size inside `draw` makes the
recording size-dependent: an animated size re-records **and** reallocates the
backing canvas every frame, which drops a magnifying dock of icons from 60 to
~25fps. A static size re-records once and costs nothing after: 120 icons
re-recording their *content* every frame run frame-bound at 16.6ms, cheaper
than the 120 text glyphs they replace.

Colour is not a rule — `ink` follows the provided text colour, so an icon beside
a muted label goes muted on its own, and a host that needs a different ink (a
menu row's check inverting on the hot row) simply sets it.

## ink
The mark's colour. Follows the provided `textColor`, so an icon beside a muted
label goes muted on its own. **The trap: that slot falls back to black platform-wide**,
so an icon in a context that never states a text colour renders black and vanishes on a
dark surface. State `ink` unless you know the context sets one — `IconHost` does it for
every icon built by name.

## weight
Stroke width in **final device pixels, not authored ones**. Divide by `unit` inside
`draw` (`d.lineWidth = weight / unit`) and the scale cancels, so the line lands at a
constant weight at every size and matches the 1px rules and text it sits among.

## unit
The 16-box-to-host-size scale factor. **Multiply the path by it; divide the stroke by
it.** Every icon is one path at one size, scaled — there are no per-size variants.

## isIcon
**Internal.** The marker a layout keys on to place an icon without knowing which shape
it is — not API.

## width
Sized by the provided `iconSize`, so a menu states 16 once and every icon in it answers; a use site may set its own.

## height
Square, always — the height follows the width.

## iconSize
The mark's size, in px — a **provided value** (a host states it once, every icon beneath
answers): defaults to the nearest provided `iconSize`, overridable at the use site.

## textColor
The effective text colour the mark's `ink` follows — a **provided value**, so an icon
beside a muted label goes muted on its own; set `ink` to override.
*/

/*
# IconHost — a named icon, materialized

   A control names its icon (`iconLeft = TrashIcon`) rather than nesting one,
   because a control is a leaf and everything else about it is an attribute — and
   because an attribute is the one form where authored and bound are the same
   mechanism. `IconHost` is what turns that name into a live view, through the
   same `app.createView` seam a menu record's `icon` field uses.

   It reserves no space when empty, so a control's `contentWidth` measures only
   the slots that are actually filled and an icon-less button needs no special
   case.

   LIMITATION, deliberate for now: the name is consumed once, at construction.
   A control whose icon must CHANGE at runtime (a play/pause toggle) is not
   served by this yet — that needs a name-valued slot the runtime re-materializes
   on change, which is a runtime feature, not a library one. Every site in this
   corpus names its icon statically.

## kind
The icon **class name** to build (`"TrashIcon"`). `""` builds nothing and the host
collapses to zero width, so an icon-less control needs no special case. **Consumed once,
at construction** — assigning a new name later does not re-materialize the icon. A name
that is only ever computed needs `use [ Name ]` to survive the build.

## ink
The colour handed to the icon this host builds. **`createView` cannot pass attributes,
so a PROVIDED value is the only channel that reaches it** — this provides `textColor`
for exactly that. Defaults to `theme.text` rather than the platform's inherited black,
which is what stops a host-built icon from rendering invisibly on a dark surface.

## onInit
Builds the named icon. Fires once.

## width
Zero when there is no icon to host, so an empty slot reserves nothing and an icon-less button needs no special case; else the provided `iconSize`.

## height
The icon's size whether or not one is hosted, so a row's height does not jump when an icon appears.

## visible
Present only when a kind is named.

## textColor
Passes the host's `ink` down as the provided text colour, which is what the icon's drawing reads — so a control's ink decision reaches its icon.

## iconSize
The size the built icon takes — a **provided value** (a menu row 16, a button 18);
defaults to the nearest provided `iconSize`.
*/

class IconHost extends View [
    kind: string = "",

    // Size from the context: `iconSize` defaults to the nearest provided value
    // (a host states it once — a menu row 16, a button 18 — and every icon
    // beneath answers), and a use site overrides just this one.

    iconSize: number = { this.$provided("iconSize", 16) },
    width  = { classroot.kind == "" ? 0 : this.iconSize },
    height = { this.iconSize },
    y = center,
    visible = { classroot.kind != "" },

    // The ink channel. `createView` cannot pass attributes, so the only way to
    // reach the icon it builds is a provided value — and the one `Icon.ink`
    // reads is `textColor`, which the host provides here from its `ink`.
    //
    // The default matters more than it looks: an icon that inherited a bare
    // `textColor` would fall back to black — fine on a light surface by luck,
    // invisible on a dark one. The provided theme's `text` token is a floor that
    // is never invisible in either palette.

    ink: Color = { this.$provided("theme").text },
    textColor = { classroot.ink },

    onInit() { if (this.kind != "") this.createView(this.kind, ({ })) }
    ]


class Icon extends View [
    // The marker a layout keys on, so a control can place its icon without
    // caring which shape it is.

    isIcon: boolean = true,

    // Size and ink come from the context via provided values: `iconSize` defaults
    // to the nearest provided value (a menu states 16 once and every icon answers),
    // and `textColor` to the nearest provided text colour — each overridable at the
    // use site. So `iconSize`/`textColor` on the icon win, a container's provision
    // cascades, and a bare icon has a sensible floor.

    iconSize:  number = { this.$provided("iconSize", 16) },
    textColor: Color  = { this.$provided("textColor", 0x000000) },

    width  = { this.iconSize },
    height = { this.width },
    y = center,

    // Follows the effective text colour, so an icon beside a muted label goes
    // muted on its own. State `ink` directly to override — `IconHost` does it for
    // every icon built by name.

    ink: Color = { this.textColor },
    weight: number = 1.6,        // stroke width in final pixels, not authored ones

    // 16-box → host size. Multiply the path by this; divide the stroke by it, so
    // the line keeps its true weight instead of scaling with the drawing.

    unit: number = { this.width / 16 }
    ]

/*
# Core icons

The marks the chrome uses everywhere: a chevron, a check, a close, plus/minus,
and the menu's help bulb. Each is authored in a 16×16 box and scaled to the
host's `iconSize` inside its recording (see `icon.declare`).

Geometry is a property of the **set**, not of the site: one stroke weight, round
caps and joins throughout, one path per shape, so a checkmark in a `Checkbox` and
one in a `Menu` row are the same mark. Ink stays local — a menu row inverts its
check on the hot row, a checkbox always uses `accentText`.
*/



/*
# ChevronIcon

The **disclosure** mark: a menu drops, a pane opens, a select expands. Every
disclosure in the chrome is this one class turned by its `dir`, which is what makes
them agree. For a direction that is itself the state — a sort order, a trend — reach
for `ArrowIcon` instead; the two must not look alike.

## dir
The resting orientation: `"down"` (the default), `"up"`, `"left"` or `"right"`. Sugar
over `angle`.

## angle
The rotation in radians, and **the primitive, so it can be sprung** — an `Accordion`
twisty turns in step with its pane sliding open rather than snapping between two
states. The turn lives in the recording deliberately: the mark rotates inside its
16-box while the box stays put. (The View-level `rotation` attribute turns the whole
box — the wrong tool for a glyph whose frame should not move.)

## draw()
Renders the chevron. Override to replace the mark while keeping the class's role.
*/

class ChevronIcon extends Icon [
    dir: string = "down",                       // down | up | left | right
    angle: number = { classroot.dir == "up" ? Math.PI
                    : classroot.dir == "left" ? Math.PI / 2
                    : classroot.dir == "right" ? -Math.PI / 2 : 0 },

    draw(d: Draw) {
        d.scale(this.unit, this.unit)
        d.strokeStyle = this.ink
        d.lineWidth = this.weight / this.unit
        d.lineCap = "round"
        d.lineJoin = "round"
        d.save()
        d.translate(8, 8)
        d.rotate(this.angle)
        d.beginPath()
        d.moveTo(-3.5, -1.75)
        d.lineTo(0, 1.75)
        d.lineTo(3.5, -1.75)
        d.stroke()
        d.restore()
        }
    ]


/*
# ArrowIcon

An arrow, **not a chevron** — the two mean different things and must not look alike.
A chevron *discloses*; an arrow points at a direction that **is itself the state**:
sort ascending, a trend, a transfer. The shaft is what a chevron lacks. The two often
sit adjacent — a sort-direction control beside a sort-menu popper — and one shape for
both reads as a mistake.

## dir
Which way it points: `"up"` (the default), `"down"`, `"left"` or `"right"`.

## angle
The rotation in radians, sprungable like `ChevronIcon`'s.

## draw()
Renders the arrow.
*/

class ArrowIcon extends Icon [
    dir: string = "up",                         // up | down | left | right
    angle: number = { classroot.dir == "down" ? Math.PI
                    : classroot.dir == "left" ? -Math.PI / 2
                    : classroot.dir == "right" ? Math.PI / 2 : 0 },

    draw(d: Draw) {
        d.scale(this.unit, this.unit)
        d.strokeStyle = this.ink
        d.lineWidth = this.weight / this.unit
        d.lineCap = "round"
        d.lineJoin = "round"
        d.save()
        d.translate(8, 8)
        d.rotate(this.angle)
        d.beginPath()
        d.moveTo(0, 5.2); d.lineTo(0, -5.2)     // the shaft is what a chevron lacks
        d.moveTo(-3.6, -1.6); d.lineTo(0, -5.2); d.lineTo(3.6, -1.6)
        d.stroke()
        d.restore()
        }
    ]


/*
# CheckIcon

The tick — a checked menu row, a `Checkbox`'s mark, a confirmation. **Ink stays
local**: a menu row inverts its check on the highlighted row while a checkbox always
uses the accent text color, so the host sets `ink` rather than the icon assuming it.

## draw()
Renders the tick. One shape, one stroke, one join — so a checkbox's mark and a menu
row's check cannot drift apart.
*/

class CheckIcon extends Icon [
    draw(d: Draw) {
        d.scale(this.unit, this.unit)
        d.strokeStyle = this.ink
        d.lineWidth = this.weight / this.unit
        d.lineCap = "round"
        d.lineJoin = "round"
        d.beginPath()
        d.moveTo(3, 8.5)
        d.lineTo(6.5, 12)
        d.lineTo(13, 4.5)
        d.stroke()
        }
    ]


/*
# CloseIcon

The dismiss mark: a window close box, a chip's remove affordance, a dialog's corner.

## draw()
Renders the cross.
*/

class CloseIcon extends Icon [
    draw(d: Draw) {
        d.scale(this.unit, this.unit)
        d.strokeStyle = this.ink
        d.lineWidth = this.weight / this.unit
        d.lineCap = "round"
        d.beginPath()
        d.moveTo(4.5, 4.5); d.lineTo(11.5, 11.5)
        d.moveTo(11.5, 4.5); d.lineTo(4.5, 11.5)
        d.stroke()
        }
    ]


/*
# PlusIcon

Add. Pairs with `MinusIcon` at the same stroke and cap, so a stepper's two ends match.

## draw()
Renders the plus.
*/

class PlusIcon extends Icon [
    draw(d: Draw) {
        d.scale(this.unit, this.unit)
        d.strokeStyle = this.ink
        d.lineWidth = this.weight / this.unit
        d.lineCap = "round"
        d.beginPath()
        d.moveTo(8, 3.5); d.lineTo(8, 12.5)
        d.moveTo(3.5, 8); d.lineTo(12.5, 8)
        d.stroke()
        }
    ]


/*
# MinusIcon

Remove, and the partially-checked state of a tri-state box. Pairs with `PlusIcon`.

## draw()
Renders the bar.
*/

class MinusIcon extends Icon [
    draw(d: Draw) {
        d.scale(this.unit, this.unit)
        d.strokeStyle = this.ink
        d.lineWidth = this.weight / this.unit
        d.lineCap = "round"
        d.beginPath()
        d.moveTo(3.5, 8); d.lineTo(12.5, 8)
        d.stroke()
        }
    ]


/*
# LightbulbIcon

The help affordance — the one FILLED mark in a stroked set: a continuous
teardrop of glass over a three-bar tapering base.

## draw()
Renders the bulb. **This one mark is filled, and does not answer to `weight`**
— the contour carries its weight in the outline itself, so there is no stroke
to widen. The bulb keeps its own visual weight at every rung.
*/

// The one filled mark: the contour is the drawing — glass as a continuous
// teardrop, the base as three tapering bars — so `weight` has no stroke to
// act on here. No y-flip anywhere: the path counts down, like this canvas.

class LightbulbIcon extends Icon [
    draw(d: Draw) {
        d.scale(this.unit, this.unit)
        d.fillStyle = this.ink
        d.beginPath()
        d.moveTo(3.4, 4.235)
        d.bezierCurveTo(3.4, 6.876, 4.982, 7.529, 5.422, 12.115)
        d.bezierCurveTo(5.449, 12.363, 5.587, 12.521, 5.848, 12.521)
        d.lineTo(10.152, 12.521)
        d.bezierCurveTo(10.42, 12.521, 10.558, 12.363, 10.585, 12.115)
        d.bezierCurveTo(11.025, 7.529, 12.6, 6.876, 12.6, 4.235)
        d.bezierCurveTo(12.6, 1.863, 10.572, 0.0, 8.0, 0.0)
        d.bezierCurveTo(5.428, 0.0, 3.4, 1.863, 3.4, 4.235)
        d.closePath()
        d.moveTo(4.438, 4.235)
        d.bezierCurveTo(4.438, 2.379, 6.068, 1.038, 8.0, 1.038)
        d.bezierCurveTo(9.932, 1.038, 11.562, 2.379, 11.562, 4.235)
        d.bezierCurveTo(11.562, 6.209, 10.255, 6.676, 9.636, 11.483)
        d.lineTo(6.37, 11.483)
        d.bezierCurveTo(5.745, 6.676, 4.438, 6.209, 4.438, 4.235)
        d.closePath()
        d.moveTo(5.827, 14.006)
        d.lineTo(10.18, 14.006)
        d.bezierCurveTo(10.407, 14.006, 10.578, 13.827, 10.578, 13.6)
        d.bezierCurveTo(10.578, 13.38, 10.407, 13.202, 10.18, 13.202)
        d.lineTo(5.827, 13.202)
        d.bezierCurveTo(5.6, 13.202, 5.422, 13.38, 5.422, 13.6)
        d.bezierCurveTo(5.422, 13.827, 5.6, 14.006, 5.827, 14.006)
        d.closePath()
        d.moveTo(8.0, 16.0)
        d.bezierCurveTo(9.066, 16.0, 9.953, 15.477, 10.021, 14.687)
        d.lineTo(5.985, 14.687)
        d.bezierCurveTo(6.034, 15.477, 6.927, 16.0, 8.0, 16.0)
        d.closePath()
        d.fill()
        }
    ]

/*
# TextLabel

A `Text` that centers its ink in its parent's height — the vertical placement a
*label* wants, as opposed to a paragraph. Use it for the text inside a control
or any centered caption; use plain `Text` for flowing copy.

Why it exists. `y = center` on a plain `Text` centers the geometric box (the
ordinary meaning, matching every other view). But a label sitting in a box wants
its **letterforms** optically centered, not the font's box with its asymmetric
ascent/descent leading — otherwise the text reads a hair low. `TextLabel`
supplies a `y` that centers the cap band (cap-top to baseline), the optical
centre for a label:

    y = { parent.height / 2 - this.baseline + this.capHeight / 2 }

That expression cap-centres the label: the ink sits centred by its cap band rather
than by its box, which is what reads as centred for a label. It is written out here,
once, instead of at every use site. It is a plain constraint over the Text's own live
metric facts
(`baseline`, `capHeight`, measured from the effective font), so it re-centers
when the font, the size, or the parent's height changes. Override `y` on an
instance to opt out.

The centre is the cap band because that is what the platform control themes
(Cupertino, Mountain View, Redmond) are matched against.

## y
Centres the ink on the parent's height by its cap band — baseline and cap height — rather than by the line box, which is what a label beside a control wants and a paragraph does not.
*/

class TextLabel extends Text [
    y = { parent.height / 2 - this.baseline + this.capHeight / 2 }
    ]

/*
# Menu

The record-driven menu: **items are data** — the component arranges; the
author never composes rows. The standard record covers real OS menus:

    { id, label, key?, icon?, enabled?, checked?, divider?, submenu?, kind?, props?, minWidth? }

- `key` renders right-aligned — display only; the menu registers no shortcut.
- `icon: "ClassName"` names an icon class for the leading column, and the label
  shifts right to make room — the same vocabulary `Segmented`'s choices use.
  One field covers every mark, including the ones no font gives you; a computed
  name needs its class kept with `use [ Name ]`, since no static reference
  reaches it.
- `enabled: false` dims the row (theme.disabledOpacity) and refuses pick.
- `{ divider: true }` is a separator line.
- `submenu: [ …records… ]` marks a cascade (the ▸ arrow).
- `kind: "ClassName"` renders the row's content with a named author class
  (app.createView — keep data-only classes with `use [ Name ]`), passed
  `props` as its datapath context. Behavior stays the row's: highlight,
  pick, keyboard are the menu's, always.
- `minWidth` is the room a row needs when it has no label to measure — a
  `kind:` row's own content. The panel is at least this wide; a longer label
  elsewhere still wins. Only a custom row needs it.

Declared once, opened by many: rows carry
`onContextMenu(e) { app.rowMenu.openAt(this, e) }`; the menu's `items`
constraint derives from `opener` — per-row variation with zero per-row
instances, live while open. `openAt` point-positions (the context-menu
rule); `openFor` drops below a control (the attached-menu rule); both
raise the menu (promotion — order is a slot) and clamp inside the app.

Dismissal: the backdrop (a full-app child under the panel) — a press
outside closes **and** is swallowed, the Mac rule; Escape closes; pick closes after delivery.

```declare
App [ width = 320, height = 130,
    chose: string = "",
    edit: Menu [ items = { [ ({ id: "cut", label: "Cut", key: "⌘X" }),
                            ({ id: "copy", label: "Copy", key: "⌘C", checked: true }),
                            ({ divider: true }),
                            ({ id: "paste", label: "Paste", enabled: false }) ] },
        picked(id: string) { app.chose = id }
        ],
    Button [ x = 20, y = 20, label = "Edit", menu = { app.edit } ],
    Text [ x = 20, y = 74, text = { app.chose == "" ? "nothing picked" : "picked: " + app.chose } ]
    ]
```

## items
The rows, as **records — never children**. A menu arranges its own rows, so handing it
views is not merely discouraged, there is nowhere to put them. The record is
`{ id, label, key?, icon?, enabled?, checked?, divider?, submenu?, kind?, props?, minWidth? }`;
a plain array is fine (no `Dataset` required). Because it is an ordinary attribute it
can be a constraint — **derive it from `opener` and one menu serves every row of a
table**, live while it is open.

## opener
The view this menu was opened for, set by `openAt`/`openFor` and cleared on close.
**The key to declaring one menu and opening it from many places**: read it in the
`items` constraint to vary the rows per opener, with no per-opener instance.

## shown
Whether the menu is up. Read it; **open through `openAt`/`openFor` rather than
assigning it**, or the menu appears unplaced, unraised, and without its keyboard claim.
Closing by assignment skips the cascade teardown for the same reason.

## picked()
**The delivery seam — override it at the use site.** Receives the picked row's `id`,
and the id is the whole message. Called *after* the menu has left the screen, so a slow
action can never freeze an open menu.

## openFor()
Opens the menu **anchored below a control**, flipping above it when there is not room
below and more room above — the native select discipline. The attached-menu rule; what
`Control.menu` uses.

## openAt()
Opens the menu **at the pointer**, given the serving view and the pointer event — the
context-menu rule. Clamped inside the app like any placement. `ContextMenu` wraps this
as `open`.

## close()
Takes the menu down, closes any cascade under it, and releases the keyboard claim.

## pick()
Delivers a row: **dismisses first, then delivers**, one painted frame later — the
native menu contract, and the reason a long-running action cannot leave a menu stranded
on screen. A submenu routes to the root so the whole chain closes as one.

## activeRow
The row the keyboard rover currently highlights, or null when the pointer is driving.
Read-only in practice.

## hasIcons
Whether any row carries an `icon` — which is what decides the icon gutter exists at
all. **A menu with no icons has no gutter**, and the text edge moves accordingly.

## hasChecks
Whether any row *can* be checked — a record carrying `checked`, true or false — which
is what decides the check column exists, exactly as AppKit reserves its state column
for any item with a state image to draw. A menu of plain
commands leads its text 17 in; one with a checkable row, 24.

## checkW
What the check column adds to the leading air when it exists (7 — the Mac's 25.5 vs
17.5, measured), else 0: the amount every column to its right shifts by.

## textEdge
The x every row's label starts at — one line for the whole menu, icons or not, and what
a `kind` row must align its own content to.

## width
Follows the rows: the text edge, the widest label, then the key column or the trailing
air — the metrics of a real macOS menu, measured (the longest label trails the edge by
18; a key column sits 26 clear of the longest label and ends 16 from the edge; menu bar
menus and popups measure the same). A use site's own `width` overrides; `minWidth`
floors it.

## minWidth
The narrowest a menu gets, whatever its rows measure — a two-item menu of short words
still reads as a menu.

## widestLabel
The widest row label, measured — the content the panel's width is built from.

## widestKey
The widest key equivalent, measured; zero when no row carries one, which is what
decides whether the key column exists.

## hasSubs
Whether any row opens a submenu — a cascade arrow needs its own trailing room.

## widestCustom
The widest `minWidth` any row asks for. A `kind:` row renders its own content and has no
label to measure, so it states the room it needs in its record and the panel is at least
that wide; a longer label elsewhere still wins.

## expectedHeight()
The panel's height *before it has been laid out*, measured when it exists and estimated
from the record count when it does not. The flip-above decision cannot wait for a
settle, which is why this exists.

## place()
Positions the panel from **root-space** coordinates, converting into the parent's space
and clamping inside the app — so a menu works declared at App level or inside a
component. The chain offset is snapshotted at open: menu chrome does not move while a
menu is up.

## isRoot
False on a cascade child. The root owns the backdrop, the deferred delivery, and the
Escape-closes-everything behaviour; a submenu delegates all three upward.

## rootMenu
The root of this menu's cascade chain — null on the root itself.

## child
The one lazily-created submenu instance, reused across every row that cascades. **A
`Menu` cannot declare a `Menu` child** (it would recurse), so the cascade is built by
name at first use.

## openSub()
Opens a row's `submenu`, creating the shared child menu on first use and placing it
alongside the row.

## closeSub()
Closes the cascade under this menu, if any.

## rootClose()
Closes the entire chain from wherever it is called — what Escape and an outside press
both do.

## step()
Moves the keyboard rover by ±1 over the pickable rows, skipping dividers, disabled rows
and custom-content rows, and scrolls the landing row into view.

## pickActive()
Picks the roved row — Enter's action. On a row with a `submenu` it enters the cascade
instead.

## enterSub()
Enters the roved row's submenu and puts the rover on its first row — ArrowRight's action.

## driveSub()
**Internal.** Pushes items, placement and delivery into the shared child menu.

## closeIt()
**Internal.** Null-safe close, the untyped seam across files.

## subShown()
**Internal.** Whether a cascade child is currently up, so the deeper menu takes the keys.

## rowsOf()
**Internal.** The row views of a panel body, for the rover's walk.

## revealRow()
**Internal.** Scrolls a roved row into view in a menu long enough to scroll.

## pickRow()
**Internal.** Picks or enters a specific row view.

## enterRow()
**Internal.** Enters a specific row's submenu.

## stepIn()
**Internal.** Puts the rover on a freshly opened cascade's first row.

## offX
**Internal.** The parent chain's x offset, snapshotted at open.

## offY
**Internal.** The parent chain's y offset, snapshotted at open.

## visible
Derived from `shown`, the menu's own open fact. Visibility is never set from outside — `openAt` and `openFor` set the fact, and dismissal clears it.

## selectable
Chrome, never prose: a menu's rows do not select, even inside a `selectable` region — the same provision every `Control` makes for its label.

## height
As tall as its panel, which is as tall as its rows — capped just inside the app's
height, past which the panel scrolls its rows and the rover keeps the landing row in
view.

## theme
The provided design-token record this widget styles off — a **provided value**
(the app provides it once with `App [ theme = { … } ]`; `Control` and the library
widgets read it). Reads `theme.accent` and its kin as typed members; defaults to the
house look. See `Control.theme`.
*/



class Menu extends View [
    // The design-token record, a provided value: the app provides it once and
    // this widget reads it, so `theme.x` reads below are plain typed members.
    // Default = the house look.

    theme: Theme = { this.$provided("theme", SanFrancisco) },
    visible = { this.shown },
    height = { this.panel.height },              // the panel; the backdrop deliberately overflows

    // A menu is chrome, not prose: its rows never select, even inside a
    // `selectable` region — the same provision `Control` makes for a label.

    selectable = false,

    // Width follows the rows, at a native menu's metrics: with a check column
    // the text leads the panel edge by 25.5 (textEdge, below) and the longest
    // label trails it by 17.5; with key equivalents the longest label sits 26
    // clear of the key column, which ends 16 from the edge. The widest label
    // and key are measured from the records, which is what the rows are built
    // from — a fold over data, not an aggregate over live children (which the
    // checker rightly refuses). A use site's own `width` overrides. Measured in
    // the face the rows are actually drawn in: a row's `TextLabel` sets only
    // its `fontSize` and inherits the rest, and `providedTextStyle` is that
    // inherited face, so the measurement and the run cannot disagree.

    widestLabel: number = { Math.max(0, ...(this.items || []).map((r) =>
        r.label == null ? 0 : measureText("" + r.label, this.$providedTextStyle(({ fontSize: 13 }))).width)) },
    widestKey:   number = { Math.max(0, ...(this.items || []).map((r) =>
        r.key == null ? 0 : measureText("" + r.key, this.$providedTextStyle(({ fontSize: 12 }))).width)) },
    hasSubs:     boolean = { (this.items || []).some((r) => r.submenu != null) },

    // A `kind:` row carries its own content and so has no label to measure — the
    // runs above see an empty string for it. Such a row states the room it needs
    // as `minWidth` in its record (a Help menu's search field: a capsule with a
    // placeholder is not a label), and the panel is at least that wide. Read off
    // the items (data), not the built rows, so it stays a plain fold.

    widestCustom: number = { Math.max(0, ...(this.items || []).map((r) => r.minWidth || 0)) },

    // The house floor: a menu narrower than this reads as a mistake rather
    // than as a tight fit.

    minWidth:    number = 120,
    width = { Math.max(this.minWidth, this.widestCustom, this.textEdge + this.widestLabel + (this.widestKey > 0 ? 26 + this.widestKey + 16 : this.hasSubs ? 34 : 18)) },

    items: array = null,
    opener: View = null,
    shown: boolean = false,

    // The column model: a check column exists when some row in this menu can be
    // checked — a record carrying `checked`, true or false — the way a native
    // menu reserves its state column for any item with a state image to draw;
    // a menu whose rows carry no `checked` leads its text 17 in. An icon column
    // exists only when some row carries an icon (no icons → no gutter at all);
    // and the text's left edge is one line for every row, icons or not. Custom
    // (kind) rows align their content to the same text edge.
    //   check col (iff hasChecks): x 7..24   ·   icon col (iff hasIcons): x 24..44 (17..37 without checks)
    //   text edge: 50 with icons, 24 without — 43 and 17 when no check column (the
    //   column's own increment is 7: a native menu's 25.5 against its 17.5)
    //
    // The 6px between the icon column and the text edge matches a native
    // menu's average air between icon and label, not its minimum: native
    // symbols carry side bearing, so only the widest glyph comes close to the
    // label while most sit well clear. Ours are drawn to fill their 16px box,
    // so matching the minimum would land every row at that tight extreme at
    // once, which reads as crowding.

    hasIcons:  boolean = { (this.items || []).some((r) => r.icon != null) },
    hasChecks: boolean = { (this.items || []).some((r) => r.checked != null) },
    checkW:    number  = { this.hasChecks ? 7 : 0 },
    textEdge:  number  = { (this.hasIcons ? 43 : 17) + this.checkW },

    // the cascade: one lazily-created child Menu (app.createView — a Menu
    // cannot declare a Menu child without recursing), reused across rows;
    // rootMenu threads to the chain's root (null on the root). activeRow is
    // the keyboard rover's highlight. View-typed slots can't see Menu
    // members, so all child-driving goes through any-typed method params —
    // the untyped seam, used deliberately.

    isRoot: boolean = true,
    rootMenu: Menu = null,
    child: Menu = null,
    activeRow: View = null,

    // the delivery seam — the app overrides; the id is the whole message

    picked(id: string) { },

    // the panel's height before first paint: measured when it exists, else
    // estimated from the records (the flip decision can't wait a settle)

    expectedHeight() -> number {
        const est = (this.items ?? []).length * (typeof this.theme.menuRow == "number" ? this.theme.menuRow : 26) + 10
        return Math.max(this.height, est)
        },

    openAt(v: View, e: PointerEvent) {
        const o = v.rootOrigin()
        this.place(o.x + e.x, o.y + e.y)
        this.opener = v
        this.shown = true
        Keys.navClaim(this, true)
        this.raise()
        },

    // viewport-aware: the list drops below the control; when it wouldn't fit
    // and there's more room above, it emerges above instead (the native
    // select discipline). place() still clamps whatever remains.

    openFor(v: View) {
        const o = v.rootOrigin()
        const h = this.expectedHeight()
        const below = o.y + v.height + 4
        const up = below + h > this.root.height - 4 && o.y - 4 - h >= 4
        this.place(o.x, up ? o.y - 4 - h : below)
        this.opener = v
        this.shown = true
        Keys.navClaim(this, true)
        this.raise()
        },

    // place() takes root-space targets (openAt/openFor get them from
    // `rootOrigin()` — the one scroll-aware walk, so a serving view inside a
    // scrolled pane anchors where the user sees it) and converts to
    // parent-space, so a Menu works declared at App level or inside a
    // component (MenuBar owns one). The chain offset is snapshotted at
    // open — menu chrome doesn't move while a menu is up.

    offX: number = 0,
    offY: number = 0,

    place(x: number, y: number) {
        const po = this.parent != null ? this.parent.rootOrigin() : ({ x: 0, y: 0 })
        const px = po.x
        const py = po.y
        this.offX = px
        this.offY = py
        this.x = Math.max(4, Math.min(this.root.width - this.width - 4, x)) - px
        this.y = Math.max(4, Math.min(this.root.height - this.height - 4, y)) - py
        },

    close() {
        this.closeSub()
        this.shown = false
        this.opener = null
        this.activeRow = null
        Keys.navClaim(this, false)
        },

    // A pick dismisses first, then delivers — the native menu contract: the
    // takedown is part of the gesture, so a long action can never freeze an
    // open menu on screen. Delivery defers past one paint (rAF, then a tick —
    // rAF alone runs before that frame's paint); a host with no rAF defers a
    // plain tick. Submenus route synchronously to the root: the chain closes
    // as one, and only the root defers the app-facing delivery.

    pick(id: string) {
        if (!this.isRoot) { this.picked(id); this.close(); return }
        this.close()
        const deliver = () => this.picked(id)
        const raf = (globalThis).requestAnimationFrame
        if (typeof raf == "function") raf(() => setTimeout(deliver, 0))
        else setTimeout(deliver, 0)
        },

    // ── the cascade ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

    // `row`/`r` below are typed `object` — a row is an anonymous replicated
    // template (the `datapath = :rows[]` view), whose type has no name to
    // write.

    openSub(row: object, subItems: array) {
        const o = (row).rootOrigin()
        if (this.child == null) this.child = this.root.createView("Menu", ({ isRoot: false, rootMenu: this.rootMenu != null ? this.rootMenu : this }))
        this.driveSub(this.child, subItems, o.x + this.width - 6, o.y - 5)
        },

    driveSub(c: Menu, subItems: array, x: number, y: number) {
        c.items = subItems
        c.picked = (id) => this.pick(id)         // delivery + close route through the chain to the root
        c.shown = true
        Keys.navClaim(c, true)
        c.place(x, y)
        c.raise()
        },

    closeSub() { if (this.child != null) this.closeIt(this.child) },
    closeIt(c: Menu?) { if (c != null) c.close() },
    subShown(c: Menu?) -> boolean { return c != null && c.shown },
    rootClose() { this.closeIt(this.rootMenu != null ? this.rootMenu : this) },

    // ── keyboard roving (the deepest shown menu handles the keys) ──────────

    rowsOf(b: View) -> array { return b.children },

    step(d: number) {
        const rows = this.rowsOf(this.panel.body).filter((r) => !r.divider && r.enabled && r.custom == "")
        if (rows.length == 0) return
        const i = rows.indexOf(this.activeRow)
        this.activeRow = rows[i < 0 ? (d > 0 ? 0 : rows.length - 1) : (i + d + rows.length) % rows.length]
        this.revealRow(this.activeRow)
        },

    revealRow(r: View?) { if (r != null) r.scrollIntoView("nearest") },

    pickActive() { this.pickRow(this.activeRow) },

    pickRow(r: object) {
        if (r == null) return
        if (r.sub) { this.enterSub(); return }
        r.pickSelf()
        },

    enterSub() { this.enterRow(this.activeRow) },

    enterRow(r: object) {
        if (r == null || !r.sub) return
        r.openSelf()
        if (this.child != null) this.stepIn(this.child)
        },

    stepIn(c: Menu?) { if (c != null) c.step(1) },

    keys: Keys [
        onKeyDown(e: KeyEvent) {
            if (!classroot.shown) return
            if (classroot.subShown(classroot.child)) return   // the deeper menu handles
            if (e.key == "ArrowDown") classroot.step(1)
            else if (e.key == "ArrowUp") classroot.step(-1)
            else if (e.key == "Enter") classroot.pickActive()
            else if (e.key == "ArrowRight") classroot.enterSub()
            else if (e.key == "ArrowLeft") { if (!classroot.isRoot) classroot.close() }
            },
        onKeyUp(e: KeyEvent) {
            if (!classroot.shown || e.key != "Escape") return
            if (classroot.subShown(classroot.child)) return   // the deeper menu handles
            classroot.rootClose()                             // Escape closes the whole chain (the desktop rule)
            }
        ],

    // items → rows through an internal derived dataset: the author passes a
    // plain array, and the wrap is the menu's own

    data: Dataset [ contents = { { rows: classroot.items || [] } } ],

    // the backdrop: the light-dismiss layer — a full-app press-catcher under
    // the panel; outside presses close and are swallowed

    back: View [ visible = { classroot.isRoot },
        x = { -classroot.x - classroot.offX }, y = { -classroot.y - classroot.offY },
        width = { this.root.width }, height = { this.root.height },
        onPointerDown() { classroot.rootClose() }
        ],

    // the panel

    // the panel caps at the viewport; past that the body scrolls (the long
    // list — a thousand bound options stay usable, the rover reveals as it
    // roves)

    panel: View [ width = { classroot.width },
        height = { Math.min(this.body.contentHeight + 10, this.root.height - 8) },
        cornerRadius = { typeof classroot.theme.menuRadius == "number" ? classroot.theme.menuRadius : 8 },

        // a frosted material when the theme names one (the frosted vibrancy
        // read), else the solid surface: `menuMaterial` is the translucent
        // wash, and a theme that also elects `menuBackdrop` gets true frost —
        // the panel samples and blurs what lies beneath it, wash over blur.

        fill = { classroot.theme.menuMaterial != null ? classroot.theme.menuMaterial : classroot.theme.surface },
        backdrop = { classroot.theme.menuBackdrop != null ? classroot.theme.menuBackdrop : null },
        stroke = { stroke(1, classroot.theme.line) },
        shadow = { classroot.theme.menuShadow != null ? classroot.theme.menuShadow : shadow(0, 10, 40, colorWithAlpha(0x000000, 0x38)) },

        body: View [ x = 0, y = 5, width = 100%,
            height = { parent.height - 10 },
            scrolls = y, clip = true,
            layout: SimpleLayout [ axis = y, spacing = 0 ],
            datapath = { classroot.data.value },

            View [ datapath = :rows[], width = 100%,
                divider:  boolean = { !!this.$data(["divider"]) },
                enabled:  boolean = { this.$data(["enabled"]) != false },
                sub:      boolean = { !!this.$data(["submenu"]) },
                custom:   string  = { typeof this.$data(["kind"]) == "string" ? "" + this.$data(["kind"]) : "" },

                // the row's highlight gate: the hover intrinsic under menu policy

                hot:      boolean = { this.hovered && this.enabled && !this.divider },
                height = { this.divider ? 11 : this.custom != "" ? Math.max(26, this.host.height + 8) : (typeof classroot.theme.menuRow == "number" ? classroot.theme.menuRow : 26) },
                opacity = { this.enabled ? 1 : (typeof classroot.theme.disabledOpacity == "number" ? classroot.theme.disabledOpacity : 0.45) },

                onPointerOver() {
                    if (!this.enabled || this.divider) return
                    classroot.activeRow = null           // the mouse takes over from the rover
                    if (this.sub) classroot.openSub(this, this.$data(["submenu"]))
                    else classroot.closeSub()
                    },

                // the rover's verbs — written on the row so :id / :submenu
                // resolve against this row's record

                pickSelf() { classroot.pick("" + this.$data(["id"])) },
                openSelf() { classroot.openSub(this, this.$data(["submenu"])) },

                // a `kind` row owns its own interior interactivity (the Finder
                // tag-dots idiom): no row-level pick, no row highlight — the
                // content's elements claim their own clicks (deepest sink wins)

                onClick() { if (this.enabled && !this.divider && !this.sub && this.custom == "") classroot.pick("" + this.$data(["id"])) },

                onInit() {
                    if (this.custom != "") this.host.createView(this.custom, ({ datapath: this.$data(["props"]) }))
                    if (typeof this.$data(["icon"]) == "string") this.icoHost.createView("" + this.$data(["icon"]), ({ datapath: this.$data(["props"]) }))
                    },

                // the hover highlight — inset, rounded, accent (the Mac read)

                hl: View [ x = 5, y = 1, width = { parent.width - 10 }, height = { parent.height - 2 },
                    cornerRadius = 5, visible = { (parent.hot || classroot.activeRow == parent) && parent.custom == "" },
                    fill = { classroot.theme.menuHl != null ? classroot.theme.menuHl : classroot.theme.accent } ],

                rule: View [ x = 10, y = 5, width = { parent.width - 20 }, height = 1,
                    visible = { parent.divider }, fill = { classroot.theme.line } ],

                // The check, from the shared set — the same tick `Checkbox`
                // draws. The ink stays local: a checked row inverts on the hot
                // row, which is the row's business, not the icon's.

                check: CheckIcon [ x = 7, y = center, iconSize = 12,
                    visible = { !parent.divider && !!this.$data(["checked"]) },
                    ink = { parent.hot || classroot.activeRow == parent
                          ? (typeof classroot.theme.menuHlText == "number" ? classroot.theme.menuHlText : classroot.theme.accentText)
                          : classroot.theme.text } ],

                // an authored icon-column cell (`icon`): the class renders

### Why data, and not `Segment` children

Because the sliding highlight cannot be built any other way. The pill has to know
which choice is selected and how wide each one is, and a constraint may not ask
the view tree that: `childViews` carries **set membership only**, so `.length` is
live while anything reaching into the collection is refused —
`aggregation over a reactive node collection … derive from data [DECLARE7001]`.
The compiler names the answer.

### Equal widths — a choice, not a limitation

Segments divide the control's width evenly. This is a design decision and it
could be otherwise: a `Layout`'s `place()` may aggregate over children — that is
how `SimpleLayout` sizes a variable-width row — so a strategy that placed each
segment by its own label and interpolated the pill between neighbours is
buildable. The `DECLARE7001` refusal binds constraints reaching into the view

- **A segmented control divides evenly; a row of buttons sizes to content.** The

- **The segmented convention makes it a content rule**: keep segment labels short and
  similar in length. Equal width enforces that rather than tolerating it. One long
  label makes the whole control look wrong, which is the feedback you want.
- **The sliding pill.** At equal widths it translates at constant width. At
  variable widths it would have to morph its width while travelling, which reads
  as rubbery and worsens the more the labels differ. Most platforms never meet
  this, because their highlight pops.

its labels.** Set `width`, or accept `segMin × choices.length`.

right place instead of skating across the bar on every layout change. The chosen

# WrappingLayout — a flow that wraps to new rows

A horizontal flow that **wraps**: children run left to right `spacing` apart,
and when the next one would overflow the view's width it drops to a new row
(`lineSpacing` down; -1, the default, means "same as spacing"). With room for
one row it is a plain row; as the view narrows it stacks — cards that reflow
on a phone with no media query. It owns both axes of each child (a flow is
2-D); sizes stay the children's own. `justify`
sets each finished row along the flow — `start`, `center`, `end`, or `fill`,
which spreads a row's slack into its gaps the way justified text does;
`indent` and `hangingIndent` inset the first row and every row after it, the
two shapes a paragraph takes.

Division of labor: this is the tool for uniform, replicated collections
that reflow by fitting. Managing named regions per width tier is
ResponsiveLayout's.

Written in Declare over the Layout kernel — the whole strategy is place().

**Padding is the view's** (`View.padding`), and a flow answers to it on
both axes: rows **wrap at the content width** — the room between the left and
right insets, never the view's own width — and a view that sizes itself from
the flow grows by the vertical pair, so no row runs under the inset.

```declare
box: View [ x = 20, y = 20, width = 260,
    layout: WrappingLayout [ spacing = 8, lineSpacing = 8 ],
    View [ width = 70, height = 26, cornerRadius = 6, fill = steelblue ],
    View [ width = 110, height = 26, cornerRadius = 6, fill = cadetblue ],
    View [ width = 90, height = 26, cornerRadius = 6, fill = slategray ],
    View [ width = 120, height = 26, cornerRadius = 6, fill = darkslateblue ]
    ]
```

## spacing
The horizontal gap between children in a row.

## lineSpacing
The vertical gap between rows. **`-1` (the default) means "same as `spacing`"**, so a
uniform grid needs one number rather than two kept in step.

## justify
How a finished row sits along the flow: `start` (the default, left), `center`, `end`
(right), or `fill` — the row's slack is spread evenly into the gaps between its
children, so every full row ends flush at the right edge, as justified text does. As
in text, the last row is left at `start` under `fill` (a ragged last line), and a row
of one child has no gap to widen and stays put. A bare literal.

## indent
The first row's inset from the left, in pixels — a paragraph's first-line indent. The
first row's usable width shrinks by it; later rows are unaffected (see `hangingIndent`).

## hangingIndent
The inset of every row after the first — a hanging indent, the shape of a bibliography
entry or a wrapped signature whose continuation lines step in under the name. The two
compose: `indent` sets where the first row starts, `hangingIndent` where the rest do.

## align
Where each child sits **within its row**: `start` (the default — the row's top),
`center`, `end`, or `baseline`, which sits every child in the row on one baseline — a
`Text` reports its own, a composite **declares** which part carries it
(`baseline: number = { cap.y + cap.baseline }`), and a child that declares none is
refused by name and placed at the row's top. A row's height grows to hold the
baseline-shifted children. When the flow **never wrapped** — one row, which is the whole
content — `center` and `end` align it in the view's own height instead, so a single row
in a `height = 90` bar really sits in the middle of it; a view that derives its height
from this flow keeps the row as the band. A bare literal.

## place()
Runs the flow, wrapping when the next child would overflow the view's width. **It owns
both axes of each child** — a flow is 2-D — while sizes stay the children's own. A child
never wraps when it is first in its row, so one over-wide child overflows rather than
looping forever. Each finished row starts at its indent, is justified along the flow, and
has its children aligned across it, in one pass over the row.
*/

class WrappingLayout extends Layout [
    spacing: number = 0,
    lineSpacing: number = -1,
    justify: Justify = start,
    align: CrossAlign = start,
    indent: number = 0,
    hangingIndent: number = 0,

    place() {
        // the room to wrap in — the view's content box, its width less its own padding
        const w = this.contentExtent("width")
        const sp = this.spacing
        const ls = this.lineSpacing < 0 ? sp : this.lineSpacing

        const al = this.align
        const ind0 = Math.max(0, this.indent)
        const indN = Math.max(0, this.hangingIndent)

        let rowBase = 0

        // children across it, and answer the row's final height — which grows
        // under baseline alignment, since children shift down to the line.
        // `rowW` is where the row's content ends (its indent included); `last`
        // says whether it is the flow's final row, which `fill` leaves ragged.
        const finish = (end, rowW, last) => {
            const slack = Math.max(0, w - rowW)
            if (slack > 0 && (jf == "center" || jf == "end")) {
                const off = jf == "center" ? slack / 2 : slack
                for (let j = rowStart; j < end; j++) out[j].x = out[j].x + off

                // the row's first moves by k shares
                let n = 0
                for (let j = rowStart; j < end; j++) if (kids[j].visible) n = n + 1
                if (n > 1) {
                    const share = slack / (n - 1)
                    let k = 0
                    for (let j = rowStart; j < end; j++) { if (!kids[j].visible) continue; out[j].x = out[j].x + share * k; k = k + 1 }
                }

            let lineH = rowH
            if (al == "baseline") {

                for (let j = rowStart; j < end; j++) {
                    if (!kids[j].visible) continue
                    const top = bases[j] == null ? 0 : rowBase - bases[j]
                    lineH = Math.max(lineH, top + heights[j])
                }
            }
            // A flow that never wrapped is not a row inside a stack of rows —
            // it IS the view's content, so center/end align it in the view's
            // own cross extent (`viewExtent` answers 0 when that extent is
            // measured from these children, and the row height stands). With
            // two or more rows the band is the row, as a wrapped flow's must
            // be: there is no `align-content` here to spread the leftover.
            if (rowStart == 0 && last && (al == "center" || al == "end")) lineH = Math.max(lineH, this.viewExtent("height"))
            for (let j = rowStart; j < end; j++) {
                if (!kids[j].visible) continue
                let off = 0
                if (al == "center") off = (lineH - heights[j]) / 2
                else if (al == "end") off = lineH - heights[j]
                else if (al == "baseline") {
                    if (bases[j] != null) off = rowBase - bases[j]
                    else this.refuseBaseline(kids[j])
                }
                out[j].y = out[j].y + off
            }
            return lineH
        }
        for (let i = 0; i < kids.length; i++) {
            const c = kids[i]
            if (!c.visible) { out.push({ x: cx, y: cy }); heights.push(0); bases.push(null); continue }   // skipped: reclaim its slot
            // the child's footprint (scale/rotation composed, position-free —
            // place() must not read the x/y it writes), and the transform's own
            // lead offset, compensated so the visible box lands on the flow
            const f = (c).footprint()
            const cw = f.width
            const ch = f.height
            const leadX = f.x
            const leadY = f.y
            // wrap when this child (with its leading gap) would overflow — never
            // on a row's first child, so one over-wide child just overflows
            if (!firstInRow && cx + sp + cw > w) { const lh = finish(i, cx, false); cx = indN; cy = cy + lh + ls; rowH = 0; rowBase = 0; firstInRow = true; rowStart = i }
            if (!firstInRow) cx = cx + sp
            out.push({ x: cx - leadX, y: cy - leadY })
            heights.push(ch)
            const b = (c).baseline
            bases.push(typeof b == "number" ? b : null)
            if (al == "baseline" && typeof b == "number") rowBase = Math.max(rowBase, b)
            cx = cx + cw
            rowH = Math.max(rowH, ch)
            firstInRow = false
        }
        finish(kids.length, cx, true)   // the last (or only) row — ragged under fill
        return out
        }
    ]

        // hiding what doesn't match, not by bolding what does); the scan is
        // timed and the number rides out with the value — pure, no clocks
        let searchMs = 0

            const needle = query.trim().toLowerCase()
